performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
question: How can stillness and sudden outcry belong to the same musical argument?
intro: The central Elegia recalls the first movement’s slow introduction, surrounding its lament with separate layers of rustling accompaniment and exposed calls. Its strongest outbursts grow from a nearly motionless background.

sections.label: Quiet frame
sections.mNote: low-string memory and separate wind figures

sections.label: First lamenting span
sections.mNote: the sparse opening gathers sustained melodic weight

sections.label: Withdrawal
sections.mNote: a low-level passage separates the larger accumulations

sections.label: Renewed ascent
sections.mNote: a new accumulation after the withdrawal

sections.label: Climactic span
sections.mNote: the largest recorded crest comes late in the central argument

sections.label: Quiet frame recovered
sections.mNote: the opening type of texture returns, altered and extended

cues.title: Remembering the low strings
cues.text: The Elegia begins low in the orchestra, recalling the sound and material of the first movement’s introduction. The memory is a structural link across the concerto, not a quotation of an external song.
cues.evidence: Score p. 47, compared with p. 1: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Rodda discusses the thematic recall: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. The cached Elegia analysis begins at a low relative level; the claim concerns the opening passage, not a matched individual note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Different speeds at once
cues.text: Listen for the difference between a sustained background and the shorter figures moving across it. The surface can remain busy while the larger phrase seems almost suspended.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 47–50 juxtaposes sustained strings, wind runs and harp figures: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Analysis places this within the opening span, but does not separate the instruments or identify a particular run at 0:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The foreground gains weight
cues.text: Around this change, the previously restrained sound becomes more forceful. Keep the quiet opening in memory: the increase matters because it grows from such a lightly occupied space.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/bartok-concerto-orchestra-elegia.txt: strong novelty at 1:12, with level rising from −26.2 dB at 1:10 to −17.5 at 1:15. The feature establishes a broad change, not an instrument entrance.

cues.title: A sudden widening
cues.text: A brief withdrawal makes the next swell unusually abrupt. Follow the whole rise rather than mistaking its loudest instant for a separate episode.
cues.evidence: The Elegia report moves from −28.1 dB at 1:50 through −15.2 at 1:55 to −9.2 at 2:00; novelty peaks at 1:56. No harmonic resolution is inferred from that increase.

cues.title: Composing at Saranac Lake
cues.text: Bartók wrote the concerto between August and October 1943 while staying at Saranac Lake, New York. Ill health formed part of those circumstances, but it does not turn each musical outcry into a documented episode from his life.
cues.evidence: Rodda’s account: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf; dates 15 August–8 October discussed with bibliography at https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto . Context is not presented as a private programme.

cues.title: Keeping a phrase through retreat
cues.text: The sound drops back sharply after the preceding span. Try to retain the phrase’s direction as its weight disappears: quietness need not mean that the argument has reached rest.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −14.2 dB at 3:05 to −29.1 at 3:10, staying relatively quiet through 3:40. This supports withdrawal, not a claimed cadence or general pause.

cues.title: The composer’s central death-song
cues.text: In his programme note, Bartók called this movement a “lugubrious death-song”. It occupies the centre of the five-movement work, between the paired-wind scherzo and the interrupted intermezzo.
cues.evidence: Bartók’s explanation and the complete movement sequence are reproduced in Rodda’s note: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. His phrase describes the movement as a whole; no individual subject of mourning is supplied.

cues.title: A crest and a recoil
cues.text: The renewed ascent has a sharp internal recoil. Listen to how the pressure is released briefly before the music starts gathering again, rather than hearing one uninterrupted crescendo.
cues.evidence: The report gives −10.0 dB at 4:10, −23.7 at 4:20 and −13.4 at 4:25, with novelty peaks at 4:10 and 4:22. Measurements support the local contour only.

cues.title: Towards the strongest outcry
cues.text: The later central span grows into the movement’s strongest recorded crest. Compare its sustained weight with the more isolated swells earlier in the movement.
cues.evidence: The report marks novelty at 5:02, levels −8.4 and −8.6 dB at 5:05 and 5:10, and its highest five-second window at 5:30 (−7.3 dB). This is a within-file level comparison, not an absolute orchestral dynamic.

cues.title: Letting the outcry subside
cues.text: The loud passage does not lead directly to the final silence. Its withdrawal makes room for another kind of sound: thinner, more separated and closer to the opening frame.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −7.3 dB at 5:30 to −30.6 at 5:50 and −37.6 at 5:55. Score pp. 64–65 supplies the subsequent thinning and recovery of opening textures: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Broad passage placement only.

cues.title: The frame is not unchanged
cues.text: The later quiet music recovers the opening’s layered manner, with moving wind figures above sustained support. It is a return of texture, not a demand to hear every earlier note repeated exactly.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 65–67, particularly bars 99–118: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 5:54, 6:00 and 6:16 locates the broad transition into the closing frame; no single return bar is claimed at 6:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An early Pittsburgh commitment
cues.text: Reiner conducted the concerto in Pittsburgh in January 1946, then recorded it the following month. Bartók had died the previous September; the record documents the work’s early life without its composer present.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz identifies the Pittsburgh performances of 18 and 20 January and recording of 4–5 February 1946: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf . Bartók’s death in September 1945 is documented in the Pittsburgh programme notes: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: The last retreat
cues.text: The closing frame still contains a small late rise before it disappears. Follow that remaining contour rather than treating the whole ending as a uniform fade.
cues.evidence: The report rises to −13.2 dB at 7:20, then falls to −26.4 at 7:30 and −36.8 at 7:45. Score p. 67 closes with exposed piccolo, muted horn and thinning strings: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Instrument colours are score-based, not separately measured at 7:26.

transitions.title: A background becomes a foreground
transitions.how: The opening’s separate figures and sustained background begin to carry a more insistent melodic argument. Greater orchestral weight changes the scale of the sound without erasing the low-register material that links this movement with the first.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 47–53: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Strong novelty at 1:12 and level increase over 1:10–1:20 anchor this broad change; the precise first lamenting phrase is not bar-synchronised.

transitions.title: A sharp attack leaves a quieter field
transitions.how: The horn chord drops sharply from its attack into a quiet sustained sound. Oboes and clarinets oscillate above quick pizzicato figures in two solo cellos, while upper-string tremolo and tam-tam resonance extend the background. The preceding weight has not become silence: different articulations keep the field moving at a much lower level.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 58–59, from bar 54: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Móricz explains the printed horn stopping/muting ambiguity at bar 54: https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf . The report drops from −14.2 dB at 3:05 to −29.1 at 3:10. That contour anchors the passage approximately; the precise horn technique used by this recording is not independently established.

transitions.title: A viola line replaces the suspended field
transitions.how: The wind oscillations and string tremolo subside. After the sparse pizzicato punctuation, violas take up a connected, expressive line marked Poco agitato, mosso, molto rubato. Muted violins and the two harps answer with shorter figures. The join therefore recovers melodic direction by changing articulation and foreground, not merely by making the preceding chord louder.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 59–60, bar 62 and following: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 3:36 and 3:44 surrounds a trough at 3:35–3:40 and renewed level at 3:45. The score’s successive duration marks place bar 62 after the earlier 54–61 field; the 3:44 anchor remains approximate.

transitions.title: High chords answer the moving lower line
transitions.how: A wind-led line gives way to more sharply divided orchestral layers. High flute and violin chords repeat above the connected motion of clarinets, bassoons and lower strings. The contrast between chordal attacks and continuing lower lines enlarges the outcry; the whole orchestra need not play one unison melody to sound collectively forceful.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 62–64, Tempo I and the repeated chords from bar 86: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. The report rises from −22.4 dB at 4:50 to −8.4 at 5:05, with novelty at 5:02. The printed cumulative duration marks support this approximate region; no individual chord is claimed at the anchor.

transitions.title: The opening texture survives the outcry
transitions.how: The climactic weight falls away and the more separated texture of the opening returns. Wind figures move above sustained support; the final pages continue to change rather than merely holding one quiet chord. The frame closes the movement while preserving a memory of its disturbances.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 65–67, from bar 99 and subsequent Tempo I: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf. Novelty at 5:54, 6:00 and 6:16 surrounds the deepest post-climax trough. The boundary labels a passage, not an exact thematic attack.

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, III
source.locator: Printed pp. 47–67. Broad passage snapshots, approximately located by measured level/novelty changes. Allow roughly 10 seconds around an entry. This is the printed-score orchestration, not source separation or a reconstruction of every detail in Reiner’s manuscript.

timeline.note: The low-string opening begins over restrained timpani; the other string voices accumulate successively (p. 47).
Wind calls and runs move over sustained strings and harp figures through the opening frame (pp. 47–50).
The fuller lamenting writing combines short wind gestures, brass weight and divided strings (pp. 53–55).
The Poco agitato region gives violas an expressive line amid muted violin figures and two harps; the snapshot covers the passage, not its first note (pp. 59–60).
The later central writing passes a line between winds and strings, broadening into the large outcry (pp. 62–64).
The recovered frame layers wind runs over held strings and muted horn support (pp. 65–66).
The final page thins towards an exposed piccolo line, muted horn and quiet strings, with sparse timpani and harp punctuation (p. 67).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
facts: Budapest Academy of Music, 1899–1903: piano with István Thomán, composition with Hans Koessler
Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages · Biskra, Algeria, 1913 · Turkey, 1936
Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.
